435.title: Sohila close
435.hook: five hymns to sleep on: praise, one sun, the sky's aarti, the city, now
435.howItsDone: Sikhs read or listen to Kirtan Sohila every night before sleep, and in gurdwaras it is recited as the Guru Granth Sahib is closed and carried to rest in the sukhasan ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rehat Maryada; your line was going home. Today we close Kirtan Sohila.

Every night in a gurdwara there's a quiet moment most visitors never see. The evening singing ends. The Guru Granth Sahib, open since dawn, is closed, wrapped in cloth, and carried with care to its resting room, often lifted on someone's head while the sangat stands. The ceremony is called sukhasan, the position of rest. And as the scripture goes to rest, the words in the air are Sohila. Two weeks ago we opened these five hymns. Tonight, the whole of it.
screen: `THE SCRIPTURE IS CLOSED.` → `SUKHASAN: THE POSITION OF REST.` → `THE WORDS IN THE AIR: SOHILA.`

segments.voice: Here are the five, the way you might remember them lying in the dark. One, Guru Nanak: the house of praise. Jai ghar keerat: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on, sing. And the wedding at its end: the date written, friends pouring oil at the door, the bride called. Two, Guru Nanak: six schools, six teachers, six teachings, one Guru of gurus in many forms; many seasons, one sun. Three, Guru Nanak: the sky's aarti. Gagan mai thaal: the sky the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls, the wind the fan, the forests the flowers. Four, Guru Ram Das: the city. Kaam karodh: desire and anger crowd the body's streets, the thorn of ego pricks with every step, and meeting the holy breaks them up. Five, Guru Arjan: now. Karau benantee: listen, friends, life runs down day and night; this is the time to serve; make me the dust of the holy's feet. Look at the movement. A doorway, the calendar, the sky, back inside the body, then a friend leaning close. Praise, unity, wonder, honesty, urgency. And then sleep. That's the shape Sikhs lie down inside every night, and the same shape sung when a life is done: a whole evening, and a whole life, held between praise at the beginning and humility at the end.
screen: `ONE: THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.` · `TWO AND THREE: ONE SUN, THE SKY'S AARTI.` · `FOUR: THE CITY OF THIEVES.` · `FIVE: NOW IS THE TIME.` · then, large: `SLEEP IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Walk through the five in your mind, the house, the sun, the sky, the city, the friend, and give each one a breath. On the last breath, picture the day being wrapped and laid to rest, like the scripture at sukhasan. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
Sukhasan, the position of rest: as the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest each night, Sohila is sung, five hymns by three Gurus said at bedtime and at the end of a life.
Your line: sleep in praise. Praise first, humility last, and rest in between. Two weeks of Sohila, done.

436.title: The jewel of peace
436.hook: Sukhmani means the jewel of peace; many read it daily or in groups when life is hard
436.carry: resting in the middle of it
436.howItsDone: Some Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily, often in the morning, and families and sangats gather to read it together in times of illness, grief, celebration and new beginnings, such as moving into a new home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukhasan, the position of rest; your line was sleep in praise. Today a new bani begins, and it will stay with us a while.

A family has just moved into a new house. Boxes still line the hall, but before the furniture is in place, a few relatives sit together on the floor, each holding a small book, reading aloud in a low, steady rhythm. The same scene can turn up the night before an exam, in the month after a funeral, in a week of bad news; sometimes it's a circle of neighbors who meet every week to do just this. They're reading Sukhmani Sahib, a bani Sikh families turn to when life is hard, and when it's new.
screen: `A NEW HOUSE, BOXES IN THE HALL.` → `PEOPLE READING ALOUD TOGETHER.` → `THE BANI THEY REACH FOR: SUKHMANI.`

segments.voice: Sukh means peace, comfort, ease, the opposite of dukh, pain. Mani means a jewel; some also hear man, the mind, in it. So Sukhmani is the jewel of peace, or the peace of the mind. Sahib is added out of respect. It was composed by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who wrote Sohila's last hymn and compiled the scripture. Tradition says he wrote it at a quiet pool near Amritsar called Ramsar, around the time the scripture was being gathered. It's in Raag Gauri, beginning on Ang 262 of the Guru Granth Sahib. And it's long: twenty-four sections, each opening with a short salok, followed by eight stanzas. Near the beginning, Guru Arjan names the bani himself. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devoted. Notice what that says peace is. Not a feeling you chase, or a place you reach once the problems are solved. Peace is the Name, remembering God, and it rests in a mind the way a jewel rests in a box. That's why families open it when life is hard. The hospital room doesn't change. The test is still tomorrow. But the Sikh hope is that something steady can rest in the middle of it. Over the next hundred days, we'll walk through Sukhmani section by section.
screen: `SUKH: PEACE. MANI: A JEWEL.` · `GURU ARJAN, AT RAMSAR.` · `TWENTY-FOUR SECTIONS, EIGHT STANZAS EACH.` · `PEACE RESTS IN A MIND.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Picture one of those living rooms, people side by side, books open, voices low, or play the first minute of a Sukhmani Sahib recording, just for the sound. Let the steadiness reach you, and find one tight place in your body and let it soften. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
Sukhmani. The jewel of peace: Guru Arjan's long bani of twenty-four sections, read daily by some Sikhs and in groups when life is hard.

437.title: How people read it
437.hook: it takes around ninety minutes; many read one ashtpadi a day
437.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
437.howItsDone: Some Sikhs read the whole of Sukhmani Sahib daily or weekly; others read one ashtpadi a day, and families and groups sometimes divide the twenty-four ashtpadis among themselves to complete it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani, the jewel of peace; your line was resting in the middle of it. Today, how people actually read a bani this long.
screen: `SUKHMANI — RESTING IN THE MIDDLE OF IT.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is long. Read aloud at an unhurried pace, it fills a good stretch of a morning. So how does anyone with a job, children and a commute read it at all? A grandmother up before dawn may read the whole of it, every day. A nurse on night shifts may not have that much quiet time in a week. Both can call Sukhmani their bani. The answer isn't a trick. It's in how the text was built, eight stanzas at a time.
screen: `A LONG BANI, A SHORT MORNING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND A NURSE.` → `THE ANSWER IS IN THE STRUCTURE.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is made of twenty-four ashtpadis. Asht is eight; pad is a stanza or verse. So an ashtpadi is an eight-stanza section. Each opens with a short salok, two lines that set the theme, and then the eight stanzas unfold it. Twenty-four times eight is one hundred ninety-two stanzas in all. That structure is a gift to a busy person. An ashtpadi is a complete thought, with a beginning, a middle and an end. You can read one in a few minutes and close the book having heard something whole. So people read Sukhmani in many ways. Some read all of it every day, often early in the morning. Some read it through once a week. Families and groups sometimes split it up, a few ashtpadis each, so that together they complete it. And some read one ashtpadi a day, so the whole bani comes round in twenty-four days. Sikh tradition doesn't set one required pace for Sukhmani. What matters, in the bani's own words, is that the Name rests in the mind. A rushed reading of all twenty-four isn't the goal; an attentive reading of one is a real reading. That's the pace we'll take here: one ashtpadi at a time, its salok first, then a few days with its stanzas, then a day for living it.

segments.voice: Think about your actual week, not an ideal one, and find a quiet ten minutes: Sunday before anyone's up, a lunch break in the car, the bus home. Picture yourself there, reading eight stanzas slowly, then let the plan go and just breathe, as if that slot had already arrived. If you pray, say Waheguru once.

438.title: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
438.hook: aad gure namah: I bow to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru (Sukhmani 1)
438.howItsDone: Sikhs who read Sukhmani Sahib begin with this salok of four bows, and Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib when they come into its presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was one ashtpadi at a time. Today we open the first one, starting with its salok.

Before a match, a wrestler in a Punjabi village touches the earth of the pit, then his forehead. A musician touches the strings before playing; a dancer bows to the floor. Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib when they come into its presence. Each begins a serious thing by lowering the head a little, first. Sukhmani begins like that too. Before a single teaching, before peace or Name or anything else, Guru Arjan bows. Four times.
screen: `A WRESTLER TOUCHES THE EARTH.` → `SERIOUS THINGS BEGIN WITH A BOW.` → `SUKHMANI OPENS: FOUR BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok that opens Sukhmani. Aad gure namah. Jugaad gure namah. Satgure namah. Sri gurdeve namah. Each line ends with namah, a word of homage: I bow, I salute. So the salok is four bows, each to a slightly different face of the same Guru. Aad gure: the Guru of the beginning, the primal Guru, there before anything began. Jugaad gure: the Guru through all the ages, jug being the great ages of time. Satgure: the True Guru. And Sri gurdeve: the great, divine Guru, the Guru who shines. Who is this Guru? In the Sikh reading of this salok, the Guru is God, the One who teaches. Sikhs also honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru's voice in the world, but here the bows go to the One beyond time. Listen to how the salok moves: from the very beginning, across all ages, to what is true, to what shines. A bow that travels from the first moment to this one. Some listeners hear an echo of Japji's opening salok, which praises the One true in the beginning and true through the ages; Guru Arjan sets Sukhmani in the same frame. And notice the order he chooses. The jewel of peace doesn't begin with peace. It begins with bowing. Peace, the bani suggests, starts with the head a little lower than before.

segments.voice: Sit up comfortably, breathe in, and as you breathe out let your head lower slowly, chin toward your chest, as far as feels easy. Stay a breath or two, noticing what it's like to be a little lower, then rise; repeat it four times if you like, one for each line. If you pray, whisper aad gure namah.

439.title: Remember, and find peace
439.hook: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remember, remember, and find peace (Sukhmani 1)
439.howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, alone or together in the sangat; some use a mala of beads to count, and some keep the Name going through the day's ordinary tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, namah, and your line: I bow. Four bows open Sukhmani. Today, the first stanza, and the word the whole bani rests on.
screen: `I BOW — FOUR BOWS TO THE GURU.`

segments.voice: How do you remember a phone number someone just told you? You say it again. And again, under your breath, all the way to the pen. How do you remember a person who has died? You say their name, tell their stories, keep their photo where you'll see it. A lot of remembering is repetition: not one grand act, but something done again and again until it becomes part of you. That's how the first stanza of Sukhmani begins: with one word, said three times in a row.
screen: `A PHONE NUMBER, SAID AGAIN.` → `A NAME, A STORY, A PHOTO.` → `REMEMBERING IS REPETITION.`

segments.voice: The first stanza opens: simro simar simar sukh paavo. I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. Then, in paraphrase: the troubles and anguish of the body are erased. The word under all of it is simran, remembrance. In Sikh life, simran means remembering God, and in practice it often means repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, again and again. Listen to how the line does what it describes. Simro, simar, simar: three beats before the reward arrives. Sukh paavo: I find peace. Sukh, the same sukh as in Sukhmani. So the jewel of peace this bani is named for is found, right at the start, by remembering. The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: the Vedas, the Puranas and the Simritis, the great scriptures of Guru Arjan's world, were made from the one word of the Name. The person in whose heart even a tiny particle of it lives has a glory no one can count. Then it closes, as the stanzas will, in Nanak's voice: those who long only for the sight of You, save me with them. Here's what makes simran different from just thinking about God. A thought comes once and is finished. Simran is a practice, a phone number said over and over until your mouth knows it before your mind does. And the stanza promises peace in that repeating.
screen: `SIMRO SIMAR SIMAR: REMEMBER, AGAIN.` · `SIMRAN: REMEMBERING GOD.` · `THE ONE WORD THE SCRIPTURES CAME FROM.` · `A PRACTICE, NOT A THOUGHT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, FIND PEACE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say Waheguru slowly ten times, aloud or in your head, each one riding on an out-breath; if not, choose a word that steadies you, peace, or thank you, or a name you love, and repeat it the same way. Count on your fingers if it helps, and don't hurry toward ten. When you reach it, sit in the quiet afterward.

440.title: What remembering does
440.hook: in remembering God there is no pain, and death does not frighten (Sukhmani 1)
440.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the first ashtpadi with their repeated opening, prabh kai simran, and many turn to them especially in times of illness or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simran, and your line: remember, find peace. Today, the stanza that says what remembering does.

An umbrella doesn't stop the rain. It doesn't shorten the storm or change the forecast. It changes one thing: what the rain does to you. You walk the same street, in the same weather, and arrive less soaked. Much of what people carry through a hard day works like that: a hand to hold, a song, a photo in a wallet. The first ashtpadi of Sukhmani lists, line after line, what remembering God does for the one who remembers. Read closely, it sounds less like a forecast and more like an umbrella.
screen: `AN UMBRELLA DOESN'T STOP THE RAIN.` → `IT CHANGES WHAT THE RAIN DOES TO YOU.` → `WHAT REMEMBERING DOES.`

segments.voice: The phrase is prabh kai simran: in the remembrance of God. The second stanza of the first ashtpadi hangs line after line on it. In paraphrase: in the remembrance of God, one does not enter the womb again. In the remembrance of God, the pain of death flees, and death is set aside. Enemies turn back; no obstacle blocks the way. One stays awake day and night. In the remembrance of God, fear does not touch you, and sorrow does not burn. The stanzas that follow keep the drum going through the rest of the ashtpadi: in God's remembrance come wisdom, meditation and understanding; the remembering one becomes truly wealthy, truly honored. Notice what the list is doing. It isn't promising that nothing bad will happen. Sikhs who read Sukhmani in hospital rooms know that pain and loss still come. It describes what changes inside the one who remembers. Fear loses its grip. Death, which frightens everyone, is set aside: not abolished, but put in its place. Sikhs believe remembering God frees the soul from the round of birth and death, which is why the stanza speaks of the womb. And on an ordinary day, it means this: the one who remembers carries something the frightening thing can't reach.

441.title: Living ashtpadi 1
441.hook: Guru Arjan begins with the simplest practice: remember
441.howItsDone: Sikhs carry the first ashtpadi's teaching into the day by repeating Waheguru during ordinary tasks, and by joining the sangat, where Sukhmani says remembrance of God is found.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was no fear in remembering. A week's end: we closed Sohila, opened Sukhmani, bowed four times, and met simran and its drum. Today, living the first ashtpadi.
screen: `NO FEAR IN REMEMBERING.` · `A WEEK: SOHILA'S CLOSE, SUKHMANI'S START.`

segments.voice: If you were writing the great bani of peace, where would you start? A philosophy of suffering? A ladder of spiritual stages, beginner to master? A list of rules? Guru Arjan, the Guru who gathered the scripture, could have begun anywhere. He began with something a child can do, what happens whenever someone you love comes to mind. No equipment, no training, no special room. He began with remembering.
screen: `WHERE WOULD YOU START?` → `A PHILOSOPHY? A LADDER? RULES?` → `GURU ARJAN STARTS WITH REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Look back at the whole first ashtpadi. The salok bows four times. The first stanza says: remember, again and again, and find peace. The next beats the drum, prabh kai simran: in God's remembrance, fear does not touch, sorrow does not burn. Then the ashtpadi widens the circle. In paraphrase: those who remember God are truly rich, truly honored, truly at rest. Near the end it says something important about where remembering happens. In paraphrase: the remembrance of God comes in the company of the holy, and it comes to those to whom God gives it. So simran isn't a feat of willpower. It grows in company, the sangat. In this reading it's a gift as much as an effort, and in the Ardas, Sikhs ask for the gift of the Name rather than claiming it. That's a gentle place to begin. The first ashtpadi doesn't ask you to be holy. It asks you to remember, among good people, and to ask for the remembering when it won't come. On an ordinary Tuesday, living it might look like a reminder on your phone that says only: remember. Waheguru, or your own steady word, on the walk from the car. A friend you sit with who makes remembering easier. Not grand. Just repeated. In the order Guru Arjan chose, remembering comes first, and the sections ahead build on it.
screen: `THE BOW, THE WORD, THE DRUM.` · `THE ONES WHO REMEMBER ARE RICH.` · `REMEMBERING GROWS IN COMPANY.` · `A GIFT AS MUCH AS AN EFFORT.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: If your phone is near, set one reminder for later with a one-word label: remember, or Waheguru if you pray. Then put the phone face down and practice now, so the reminder has somewhere to land: a few slow breaths, the Name or your word on each one.
Sangat, the company of the holy: Sukhmani's first section in daily life: bow, remember again and again, and let the remembering grow in good company.
Your line: begin with remembering. It grows best in good company, among good people. That's a week.
